It is rewritten as `count += (err != 0);`. What can you conclude about performance from this source change alone?

options.text: A big speedup, because branches are always slow
options.explanation: Source branches are not always machine branches, and a predictable machine branch is not automatically a bottleneck.

options.text: No definite speedup or slowdown: inspect generated code and benchmark the workload
options.explanation: Correct. Both forms may compile identically. If machine code differs, prediction, dependencies, extra work and vectorisation determine the result.

options.text: It will crash, because booleans can't be added to integers in C
options.explanation: In C a comparison yields an `int` 0 or 1, so the addition is perfectly legal.

options.text: It reduces the misprediction rate from 50% to 0%
options.explanation: The source frequency is not a measured misprediction rate, and neither rate follows from syntax alone.

questions.workedExample: The comparison yields C int 0 or 1, so the updates produce the same unsigned value under the stated assumptions. This equivalence is not promised for volatile or atomic counters: +=0 still performs an access or read-modify-write. The compiler may use a branch, conditional operation or vectorisation for either form. A rare true outcome can make a retained branch predictable, but source outcome frequency alone does not specify its actual prediction accuracy. Check assembly and measure with available performance counters.

questions.prompt: A single 2-bit saturating counter is dedicated to one branch, with no history. In steady state, which outcome patterns does it predict with at least 90% accuracy?

options.text: Always taken
options.explanation: Yes: the counter saturates at 3 and predicts T every time, 100%.

options.text: Taken 9 times, then not taken once, repeating
options.explanation: Yes: only the N mispredicts (the counter drops from 3 to 2 and still predicts T), so 90%.

options.text: Strictly alternating T, N, T, N
options.explanation: No. For a trace beginning T,N, state 1 cycles 1→2→1 and misses every outcome. Starting in state 2 or 3 yields 50% steady-state accuracy; state 0 approaches that pattern.

options.text: Independent random outcomes, each taken with probability 50%
options.explanation: No: when outcomes are independent of predictor information, expected accuracy is 50%; a finite sample can differ.

options.text: Taken 99 times, then not taken once, repeating
options.explanation: Yes: one miss per 100, 99%.

questions.workedExample:
Work out misses per period for each pattern:

| Pattern | Misses | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| all T | 0 | 100% |
| 9T, N | 1 / 10 | 90% |
| T, N | 1 or 2 / 2 | 50% or 0% |
| random | ~1 / 2 | ~50% |
| 99T, N | 1 / 100 | 99% |

The 2-bit counter is good for biased branches and loop exits; it does not track phase within a period. It can score well on a biased periodic pattern without learning its exact sequence.

lessons.title: Superscalar, out-of-order and Tomasulo
lessons.summary: How modern cores finish several instructions per cycle by issuing them out of order, using register renaming, reservation stations, Tomasulo's algorithm and a reorder buffer, and what still limits them.
lessons.body:
A scalar pipeline, however well forwarded and predicted, peaks at one instruction per cycle. In this instruction-level model, sustaining CPI below 1 requires starting more than one instruction per cycle on average. That is **superscalar** execution.

In-order superscalar execution can improve throughput, but a blocked instruction can prevent younger independent work from issuing. **Out-of-order** execution finds ready work further ahead while preserving the architectural rules. The 200-cycle load used below is hypothetical, not a universal DRAM latency. In-order retirement does not imply sequentially consistent interthread memory ordering. This lesson shows how.

## Instruction-level parallelism

**Instruction-level parallelism** (ILP) is the number of instructions in a stretch of code that could, in principle, run at the same time.

```
a = b + c      # independent
d = e + f      # independent
g = a * d      # needs both
```

The first two can run together; the third must wait. ILP is limited by **true (RAW) dependences**, by branches (you can't run what you haven't fetched), and by memory latency.

## In-order superscalar

A simple in-order superscalar design can issue two instructions per cycle when pairing rules, operands and execution resources allow. Multiple issue does not itself require out-of-order scheduling.

The weakness of in-order issue: when one instruction stalls, everything behind it stalls too, even independent work.

```
lw   x1, 0(x2)    # assume a long cache miss
add  x3, x1, x4   # must wait: depends on x1
mul  x5, x6, x7   # independent, but stuck
sub  x8, x9, x10  # independent, but stuck
```

An out-of-order core runs `mul` and `sub` while the load is outstanding.

## The out-of-order pipeline

A common out-of-order (OoO) teaching design has three parts. Real designs differ in µop grouping, scheduler organisation and retirement bookkeeping:

```
IN ORDER: fetch, decode, rename,
          allocate ROB entry
              |
              v
OUT OF ORDER: scheduler waits for
              operands, issues to
              ALUs / load-store unit
              |
              v
IN ORDER: reorder buffer retires
          (commits) oldest first
```

1. **Front end, in order**: fetch (guided by the branch predictor), decode into µops, **rename** registers, and allocate tracking space in the **reorder buffer** (ROB) and in a scheduler.
2. **Execution, out of order**: each µop waits in the scheduler until its source operands are ready and a suitable unit is free, then **issues**. Results are broadcast to waiting µops.
3. **Retirement, in order**: the ROB commits results to the architectural state strictly in program order, so exceptions and mispredictions can be handled precisely.

## Register renaming

Out-of-order execution exposes the **name dependences** from lesson 3:

```
i1: mul x1, x2, x3
i2: add x4, x1, x5   # RAW on x1 (real)
i3: add x1, x6, x7   # WAW i1, WAR i2
i4: add x8, x1, x2   # RAW on i3's x1
```

i3 and i4 have nothing to do with i1 and i2; they just reuse the name x1. But if i3 ran before i1 finished, it could have its x1 overwritten by the slow `mul` (WAW), or i2 could read i3's x1 instead of i1's (WAR).

**Renaming** assigns distinct storage to simultaneously live register versions. A physical-register implementation maintains more result storage than the architectural register set. Exact counts depend on the core and ISA extensions; they are omitted without a specified implementation. A **register alias table** (RAT) maps each architectural register to the physical register holding its newest value.

This teaching renamer handles a finite straight-line sequence of ordinary register-producing operations. It has no retirement, branches, zero-register semantics or free-list reclamation; names x0… are generic, not a complete RISC-V implementation.

```python
def rename(prog, n_arch=32, n_phys=128):
    if not 0 < n_arch <= n_phys:
        raise ValueError("bad counts")
    rat = {f"x{i}": f"p{i}"
           for i in range(n_arch)}
    free = [f"p{i}"
            for i in range(n_arch, n_phys)]
    for op, dst, srcs in prog:
        s = [rat[r] for r in srcs]
        if dst not in rat:
            raise ValueError("bad dst")
        if not free:
            raise ValueError("no registers")
        rat[dst] = free.pop(0)
        print(f"{rat[dst]} = {op}"
              f"({', '.join(s)})")

rename([
    ("mul", "x1", ["x2", "x3"]),
    ("add", "x4", ["x1", "x5"]),
    ("add", "x1", ["x6", "x7"]),
    ("add", "x8", ["x1", "x2"]),
])
```

Output:

```
p32 = mul(p2, p3)
p33 = add(p32, p5)
p34 = add(p6, p7)
p35 = add(p34, p2)
```

The two x1s are now p32 and p34. Only true register dependences remain in this arithmetic trace (p32 → p33, p34 → p35), so i3 and i4 can execute while the `mul` is still running. Sources are renamed *before* the destination, so `add x1, x1, x2` correctly reads the old x1.

In a simple design without shared physical mappings or other retained references, the free list is refilled at retirement: when an instruction that overwrites x1 commits, the physical register that held the *previous* x1 can no longer be needed and is freed.

## Tomasulo's algorithm

Robert Tomasulo devised the original scheme for the floating-point unit of the IBM System/360 Model 91 (1967). Its tag-based scheduling and renaming ideas are foundational; modern implementations need not use the original structure.

Three structures:

- **Reservation stations** (RS) sit in front of each functional unit. Each holds one waiting instruction and, for each operand, either its **value** (V) or the **tag** (Q) of the reservation station that will produce it.
- A **register status table** records, for each register, which RS tag will write it next (blank if the register file value is current).
- A **common data bus** (CDB) broadcasts every result as a (tag, value) pair to all reservation stations and the register file at once.

Each instruction goes through:

1. **Issue**: take the next instruction in order, if a matching RS is free. For each source, copy the value from the register file if it is current, or else copy the producing tag. Then set the destination register's status to this RS's tag.
2. **Execute**: when both operands are values, start executing. Independent instructions overtake stalled ones here.
3. **Write result**: broadcast (tag, value) on the CDB. Every RS waiting on that tag grabs the value. The register file is updated only if its status still names this tag.

Tags distinguish producer versions, providing renaming without requiring the separate physical register file used in the preceding example. A reservation station is not literally a physical register.

### A worked snapshot

```
1: L.D   F6, 0(R2)
2: MUL.D F0, F6, F4
3: ADD.D F6, F8, F2
4: SUB.D F2, F6, F4
```

Assume enough reservation stations, ready initial registers and sufficiently long operation latencies for all four to issue before any result broadcasts. This is a schematic floating-point instruction trace, not literal IBM instruction syntax:

| RS | Op | Operand j | Operand k |
|---|---|---|---|
| Load1 | L.D | addr R2+0 | |
| Mult1 | MUL | Q = Load1 | V = F4 |
| Add1 | ADD | V = F8 | V = F2 |
| Add2 | SUB | Q = Add1 | V = F4 |

Register status: F0 ← Mult1, F2 ← Add2, F6 ← Add1.

What happens next:

- **Add1 can start immediately.** It copied F8 and F2 at issue, so it waits for neither the load nor the multiply.
- When **Load1** broadcasts, Mult1 captures the value. But F6's status says Add1, not Load1, so the **register file is not updated**. The load's F6 is now an orphan that only Mult1 needed. That is the WAW hazard with instruction 3, resolved.
- When **Add1** broadcasts, Add2 (the SUB) captures it, and F6 in the register file is updated.
- SUB overwrites F2, which ADD read. That WAR is harmless: ADD copied F2's value into its RS at issue.
- **Mult1** can finish last despite issuing second; exact completion order depends on latencies and resource availability.

### What the original lacked

The Model 91 wrote results to registers as soon as they were computed, out of order, so a fault in an earlier, slower instruction left a state where later instructions had already taken effect. It could produce **imprecise** floating-point exceptions. The original tag-and-broadcast algorithm described here lacks the modern speculative branch-recovery machinery.

## The reorder buffer

A **reorder buffer**, discussed by Smith and Pleszkun in their work on precise interrupts, is one solution. In this teaching model it is a circular queue with one entry per in-flight instruction, in program order. Real entry granularity can differ. Checkpointing and other bookkeeping are also needed for speculative recovery.

- Instructions execute out of order and write results into their ROB entry (or a physical register), not the architectural state.
- The head of the ROB **retires** (commits) only when it has completed. Retirement is in order, up to the supported retirement width per cycle.
- If the head instruction faulted, the core discards it and every younger entry, and the exception appears exactly at that instruction: **precise exceptions**.
- If a branch turns out mispredicted, every entry after it is **squashed**. The rename table is restored to its state at the branch, and fetch restarts on the right path.

This is what makes **speculative execution** safe, architecturally: wrong-path instructions execute, but never commit. But "never commits" is not the same as "leaves no trace": some microarchitectural effects, such as cache state, may persist; recovery of predictor history is implementation-dependent, which is what the Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities revealed.

### Memory ordering

Loads and stores need extra care, because whether two of them conflict depends on addresses that aren't known until they execute.

- Ordinary cacheable stores retain speculative data in a store queue or buffer until it is safe to commit. Squashing a store must not make its data architecturally visible; related address translation or ownership requests can still affect microarchitectural state.
- A load may forward bytes from the youngest matching older store when address, data and coverage requirements permit. Partial overlaps or unavailable data can require stalling or replay.
- A core may let a load pass older stores with unknown addresses (**memory disambiguation**). If required ordering was violated, recovery re-executes affected work; a full squash from the load is one implementation, not a universal mechanism.

## How big is the window?

> [!note] Product data omitted
> Exact commercial decode widths and ROB sizes are omitted because sufficiently reliable, consistently defined primary-source figures were not established here. Instruction counts, µop counts and ROB entries are not interchangeable.

For a hypothetical 80 ns miss at 4 GHz, latency is 320 cycles. Maintaining allocation at four entries per cycle while retirement is blocked would require space for roughly 1,280 entries. This is an occupancy estimate, assuming sufficient independent work and no earlier resource limit. It does not prove all real misses stall for a fixed duration. A larger window may discover independent memory accesses whose latencies overlap (**memory-level parallelism**); bandwidth and other queues still limit progress.

## Why not let the compiler do it?

**VLIW** (very long instruction word) designs expose operation grouping to the compiler, shifting much scheduling work from hardware to software. Variable memory latency makes static scheduling harder. Intel Itanium used **EPIC**, an explicitly parallel design with bundles, instruction groups, predication and speculation; it should not be reduced to a simple VLIW machine with no means to tolerate uncertain execution. A single-cause explanation of its commercial outcome is omitted because this lesson has not established evidence for one.

## The costs

- **Area and power.** Rename tables, schedulers that compare every result tag with every waiting operand each cycle (wakeup and select), and large multi-ported register files are expensive. Scheduler logic scales badly with width.
- **Diminishing returns.** Dependence chains, branch recovery, fetch limits and memory behaviour can leave issue capacity unused; achievable IPC is workload- and core-dependent.
- **Mispredictions cost more.** More speculative capacity can allow more wrong-path work, but does not by itself fix the recovery latency or amount discarded.

These costs are part of why performance per core stopped growing fast enough, leading to multicore (the final lesson of this module).

## Key takeaways
- Superscalar cores issue several instructions per cycle; out-of-order cores pick ready instructions whose execution resources and ordering constraints permit issue rather than stalling behind a blocked one.
- Register renaming maps architectural to physical registers, removing register-name WAR and WAW dependences. True register data dependences, control constraints and memory ordering still matter.
- Tomasulo's algorithm uses reservation stations holding values or producer tags, and a common data bus that broadcasts results; tags are renaming.
- The reorder buffer retires in order, supporting precise exceptions and architectural recovery with additional bookkeeping; it does not erase every speculative side effect.
- Window size matters for hiding memory latency and enabling memory-level parallelism; VLIW's static scheduling struggles with unpredictable cache misses.

questions.prompt: Which register dependences does register renaming eliminate?

options.text: RAW (true) dependences
options.explanation: RAW is real data flow: the consumer needs the producer's value. No renaming can remove that; it can only be waited for or forwarded.

options.text: WAR and WAW (name) dependences
options.explanation: Correct. These exist only because two instructions reuse the same register name. Giving each result its own physical register removes them.

options.text: All three: RAW, WAR and WAW
options.explanation: Renaming leaves RAW in place. If it removed true dependences, programs would compute the wrong answers.

options.text: Control dependences on branches
options.explanation: Branches are handled by prediction and speculation, not renaming.

questions.workedExample:
1. RAW: i2 reads what i1 wrote. Data flows, so i2 must wait. Renaming keeps this: i2 reads i1's physical register.
2. WAR: i3 overwrites a register i2 still has to read. With renaming, i3 writes a *new* physical register, so i2's input is untouched.
3. WAW: two writes to the same name. Each gets its own physical register; the RAT points to the newest.
4. So renaming removes WAR and WAW only.

questions.prompt: An out-of-order core schedules ready instructions when the required resources are available. Why might its design use a reorder buffer to retire instructions in program order?

options.text: To make instructions execute faster
options.explanation: Retirement order doesn't speed execution; it controls when results become architecturally visible.

options.text: Because functional units can only accept instructions in order
options.explanation: Execution is out of order by design; the scheduler sends any ready instruction to a free unit.

options.text: So that exceptions are precise and mispredicted work can be discarded before it changes architectural state
options.explanation: Correct. In-order commitment provides a precise architectural boundary for faults and discards uncommitted wrong-path results. It does not by itself impose sequential consistency on memory operations across threads.

options.text: To store the branch predictor's history
options.explanation: Predictor history lives in the front end; the ROB tracks in-flight instructions.

questions.workedExample:
1. Suppose instruction 10 executes before instruction 5, and then instruction 5 page-faults.
2. Without a ROB or another precise-state mechanism, immediate out-of-order register updates could expose instruction 10's result: the OS sees an impossible state (imprecise exception).
3. With a ROB, instruction 10's result waits in its ROB entry (or an uncommitted physical register).
4. Instruction 5 reaches the head, faults, and the core discards 5 to 10 and everything after. The state is precise.
5. The same mechanism undoes wrong-path work after a mispredicted branch.

questions.prompt:
This code runs on a core with a single in-order pipeline and on an out-of-order core. The load misses in the cache and takes 200 cycles.

```
lw  x1, 0(x2)
add x3, x1, x4
mul x5, x6, x7
sub x8, x9, x10
```

What does the out-of-order core do differently? Assume all four fit in the scheduling window, other operands are ready and suitable units are available; exclude value prediction.

options.text: It runs the `add` before the load completes
options.explanation: The `add` truly depends on x1, so no core can run it before the load returns.

options.text: It skips the load
options.explanation: The load must happen; skipping it would compute the wrong result.

options.text: Nothing; both cores must wait for the load before doing anything else
options.explanation: That is the in-order core's behaviour. Out-of-order cores exist to avoid it.

options.text: It executes `mul` and `sub` while the load is outstanding, then the `add` when x1 arrives
options.explanation: Correct. `mul` and `sub` don't depend on x1, so the scheduler issues them as soon as their operands are ready, filling cycles the in-order core wastes.

questions.workedExample:
1. Dependences: `add` needs x1 (from `lw`). `mul` and `sub` need only registers already available.
2. In-order core: `add` stalls, and `mul` and `sub` are stuck behind it for ~200 cycles.
3. Out-of-order core: all four enter the window; `mul` and `sub` issue immediately; `add` waits in the scheduler.
4. Retirement is still in order: `lw`, `add`, `mul`, `sub`, preserving specified architectural results; timing and other microarchitectural effects can differ.

questions.prompt:
The RAT maps each xN to pN, and the free list is p40, p41, p42, ... Rename:

```
add x1, x2, x3
sub x2, x1, x4
mul x1, x2, x1
```

What does the `mul` become?

options.explanation: Correct. add → p40 (x1 = p40). sub reads p40, p4 → p41 (x2 = p41). mul reads x2 = p41 and x1 = p40, then gets p42.
This renames the destination before reading the sources, so the mul would read its own output. Sources must be looked up first.

options.text: `mul p42, p2, p1`
options.explanation: This uses the original mappings, ignoring that add and sub already remapped x1 and x2.

options.text: `mul p42, p41, p1`
options.explanation: x2 is correctly p41, but x1 was remapped to p40 by the add.

questions.workedExample:
Step through, reading sources from the RAT before updating the destination:

```
add x1,x2,x3 -> p40 = add(p2, p3)
               RAT x1 = p40
sub x2,x1,x4 -> p41 = sub(p40, p4)
               RAT x2 = p41
mul x1,x2,x1 -> p42 = mul(p41, p40)
               RAT x1 = p42
```

The second write to x1 (p42) no longer conflicts with the first (p40), so any later reader of the old x1 still sees p40 while it is live.

questions.prompt: In Tomasulo's algorithm, the load in reservation station Load1 broadcasts (Load1, 3.5) on the common data bus. Mult1 is waiting with Qj = Load1. The register status table says F6 ← Add1. What happens?

options.text: Mult1 captures 3.5, and F6 in the register file is set to 3.5
options.explanation: Mult1 does capture it, but F6's status names Add1, a later writer. Writing 3.5 there would let an older value overwrite the newer one (a WAW error).

options.text: Mult1 captures 3.5; the register file is not updated, because a later instruction (Add1) will write F6
options.explanation: Correct. Every waiting RS with a matching tag takes the value. The register file only accepts it if its status still names that tag, which resolves the WAW hazard.

options.text: Nothing happens until Add1 finishes
options.explanation: The broadcast is consumed immediately by any station waiting on Load1.

options.text: Mult1 must re-read F6 from the register file
options.explanation: Mult1 recorded a tag at issue precisely so it doesn't have to read the register file again; it captures from the CDB.

questions.workedExample:
1. Every RS compares its Q fields to the broadcast tag. Mult1 matches Load1, so Vj = 3.5 and Qj is cleared; Mult1 may start if its other operand and the functional unit are ready.
2. The register file checks F6's status. It names Add1, meaning a younger instruction will produce the architecturally newest F6.
3. So F6 is **not** written. The load's value lives only in the stations that needed it.
4. That is register renaming via tags: the 'F6 from the load' and the 'F6 from the add' are different values with different names.

questions.prompt: A 4-wide core executes only one long chain of dependent integer adds, each with one-cycle result latency and forwarding. Ignoring loop-control, fetch and retirement overhead, what is the maximum steady-state add IPC?

options.explanation: Width is an upper bound, but only independent instructions can issue together. Each add needs the previous one's result.
That would be one instruction every 4 cycles. With 1-cycle latency and forwarding, one add can complete each cycle.
Correct. A dependence chain with 1-cycle latency allows exactly one instruction per cycle, regardless of width or window size.
No reordering can create parallelism that a single dependence chain doesn't have.

questions.workedExample: Each add needs the previous result, so at most one add starts per cycle: add IPC = 1. Independent accumulators can expose more parallelism if arithmetic reassociation preserves required semantics and enough ALUs and issue capacity exist. Four-wide decode alone does not imply four add-capable execution units.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Tomasulo's algorithm are true?

options.text: Each reservation station operand holds either a value or the tag of the station that will produce it
options.explanation: True. That V/Q pair is the core of the scheme.

options.text: Results are broadcast on a common data bus to all waiting stations and the register file
options.explanation: True. This lets every consumer pick up a result in the same cycle.

options.text: The original IBM 360/91 implementation guaranteed precise interrupts
options.explanation: False. Some Model 91 floating-point exceptions were imprecise. Later processor designs used reorder buffers or other precise-state mechanisms; this does not claim a ROB was retrofitted into Model 91.

options.text: WAR hazards are avoided by capturing the current value or its producer tag when an instruction issues
options.explanation: True. A later register write cannot replace the saved value or change the producer version named by the tag.

options.text: Instructions enter reservation stations out of program order
options.explanation: False. Issue (into the stations) is in order; only execution is out of order.

questions.workedExample:
1. V/Q per operand: **true**.
2. CDB broadcast: **true**.
3. The claim that 360/91 always guaranteed precise interrupts is **false**; some floating-point exceptions were imprecise.
4. Copy at issue removes WAR: **true**.
5. Issue is in order; execute is out of order: **false**.

Mnemonic: in order in, out of order through, (with a ROB) in order out.

questions.prompt: In a simplified 3 GHz core, a load at the ROB head has 100 ns remaining. Assume about 512 free entries, allocation at four entries per cycle, no retirement until it returns, and no earlier resource bottleneck. Roughly when does allocation stop?

options.text: The ROB hides the miss completely
options.explanation: Maintaining allocation at four entries per cycle for all 300 cycles would require 1,200 free entries. Whether independent work hides latency is a separate workload question; this model only predicts when allocation exhausts capacity.

options.text: The core stalls immediately for 300 cycles
options.explanation: Retirement is already blocked, but allocation and independent execution can continue while resources remain.

options.text: The free entries fill in about 128 cycles; allocation then waits roughly another 172 cycles
options.explanation: Correct in this occupancy model: 100 ns × 3 GHz = 300 cycles, 512 / 4 = 128, and 300 − 128 = 172. Already allocated instructions may still execute.

options.text: The load is retired early to free its entry
options.explanation: A load can't retire before its value arrives: retirement is in order and needs a completed result.

questions.workedExample: At 3 GHz, 100 ns is 300 cycles. About 512 free entries fill in 128 cycles at four entries per cycle. Allocation then waits about 172 cycles. Retirement is blocked throughout, but execution need not cease when allocation stops. Real free capacity, dependencies, other queues and memory bandwidth may change this estimate.

questions.prompt: A branch was predicted taken, and 40 wrong-path instructions have already executed and written physical registers when the branch resolves as not taken. What does the core do?

options.text: Lets them retire, then runs compensating instructions
options.explanation: Wrong-path instructions must never retire; there are no compensating instructions in hardware recovery.

options.text: Squashes every ROB entry younger than the branch, restores the rename table to its state at the branch, safely reclaims the wrong-path physical registers, and refetches from the correct path
options.explanation: Correct. Since nothing younger had committed, no architectural state changed. The RAT checkpoint (or a walk back through the ROB) restores the mappings.

options.text: Flushes only the 40 executed instructions; unexecuted wrong-path ones can stay
options.explanation: Every instruction after the branch is on the wrong path, executed or not. All are squashed.

options.text: Raises an exception to the operating system
options.explanation: Ordinary branch misprediction recovery is handled by hardware; it does not itself require an OS exception.

questions.workedExample:
1. The branch's ROB entry marks the boundary: everything younger is wrong-path.
2. Squash: discard those ROB entries, scheduler entries and store-buffer entries.
3. Restore the RAT: mappings revert, and wrong-path physical registers return to the free list when safely reusable.
4. Redirect fetch to the correct target.
5. Architectural state is untouched. Some microarchitectural effects, such as cache changes, may persist; predictor-history recovery varies, which is what the Spectre attacks exploited.

questions.prompt: An older store `sw x3, 0(x5)` hasn't computed its address yet. A younger load `lw x7, 0(x6)` is ready. The core speculatively lets the load go first. Later the store's address turns out equal to the load's. What happens? Assume aligned ordinary memory, equal access sizes, no intervening store or external writer, and a design that recovers by squashing from the load.

options.text: The load keeps its value; loads and stores can't overlap
options.explanation: The addresses overlap. The load may have read the pre-store value rather than the value required by the older store. The specified design detects the ordering violation and replays; numerical equality would not establish a general ordering guarantee.

options.text: The store is cancelled
options.explanation: The store is correct and older; it must happen. The load is what went wrong.

options.text: The core detects the violation and re-executes the load and younger work; the load must obtain the older store’s value
options.explanation: Correct under the stated recovery design. The value may be forwarded when store data is ready, or read after the store becomes visible; immediate forwarding is not guaranteed.

options.text: The program reads the old value and the OS fixes it
options.explanation: This is invisible to software and handled in hardware.

questions.workedExample: The younger load must observe the older same-address store under these assumptions. If it speculatively read stale data, the core detects the ordering violation and recovers by the stipulated squash. On re-execution it waits, forwards or reads the now-updated memory as appropriate. Other designs may use more selective replay.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine reasons that making out-of-order cores ever wider gives diminishing returns?

options.text: A scheduler may need many result-tag/operand comparisons and selection paths, making width and window expansion costly
options.explanation: True. Comparison count grows with the number of broadcast results and waiting operands in this design. Actual area, timing and power scaling depend on scheduler organisation.

options.text: Renaming introduces extra RAW dependences
options.explanation: Not a reason. Renaming removes name dependences and adds no true ones.

options.text: Real programs' true dependence chains and branches limit how much ILP exists
options.explanation: True. Dependences and control flow can prevent a workload from supplying enough independent ready operations.

options.text: A wider speculative machine can do more wrong-path work before a branch resolves
options.explanation: True as a possible cost, not a universal width-times-depth penalty. Resolution timing, dependencies and occupancy matter.

options.text: The reorder buffer forces instructions to execute in program order
options.explanation: Not a reason. The ROB only forces in-order retirement; execution is out of order.

questions.workedExample:
Separate real limits from misconceptions:

1. Scheduler complexity: real, a hardware cost.
2. Renaming adding RAW: false; renaming only removes WAR/WAW.
3. Limited ILP: real, a property of the code.
4. Additional speculative capacity can increase wasted work: a real possible cost, not a fixed scaling law.
5. ROB enforcing execution order: false; it orders retirement.

These limits, together with power, are why per-core gains slowed and designs turned to more cores.

lessons.title: The power wall and multicore
lessons.summary: Why power constraints slowed clock scaling, the physics of dynamic power and Dennard scaling, and how the industry turned to multicore, frequency scaling, heterogeneous cores and specialisation.
lessons.body:
Clock increases and microarchitectural improvements contributed to rapid single-thread performance growth before the mid-2000s. Power and thermal constraints made continuing that trend harder and encouraged multicore designs. Clock rates and single-core performance did not stop improving, and there is no universal 3–4 GHz ceiling.

> [!note] Evidence limits
> Universal cooling wattages, voltage floors, current clock-rate limits and specific cancelled-product explanations are omitted because they need product- and process-specific evidence. The power examples below are models, not operating advice or measured processor specifications.

## Dynamic power

CMOS circuits use energy charging and discharging capacitances. A common approximation for average capacitive switching power is:

```
P_dynamic = a x C x V^2 x f
```

- **a** (activity factor): average charging activity per clock cycle, consistently defined for the capacitances included in C; not simply an unweighted fraction of transistors.
- **C**: the capacitance represented by the activity model. Equivalently, sum each node’s activity × capacitance.
- **V**: supply voltage.
- **f**: clock frequency.

At fixed activity and capacitance, power is linear in frequency and quadratic in voltage. Higher frequencies may require higher voltage, but **V is not universally proportional to f**. A cubic frequency rule follows only if voltage also scales proportionally over the modelled range. Total chip power includes leakage, other switching effects and other components.

> [!example] What 15% less frequency buys
> Drop V and f by 15% each. Dynamic power scales by 0.85 × 0.85² = 0.85³ ≈ **0.61**. With unchanged activity and capacitance, capacitive switching power falls about 39%. Performance falls 15% only if throughput is proportional to frequency; total energy and total system power need separate accounting.

There is also **static (leakage) power**: current that trickles through transistors even when they are not switching. It depends on voltage, temperature and transistor design, and cannot be inferred from transistor dimensions alone.

## Dennard scaling and its end

In 1974 Robert Dennard and colleagues at IBM observed how MOSFETs scale. In the ideal constant-field model, shrink dimensions by a factor k (say 0.7 per process generation) and also scale voltage by k:

| Quantity | Scales by |
|---|---|
| Capacitance per transistor | k |
| Voltage | k |
| Frequency | 1 / k |
| Power per transistor | k² |
| Transistors per area | 1 / k² |
| Power per area | 1 (constant) |

Power per transistor is C × V² × f = k × k² × (1 / k) = k². Transistors per area rise by 1 / k². So **power density stays constant**: each generation gives more transistors, each faster, at the same watts per square millimetre. Together with Moore's law, this is what drove decades of rising clock speeds.

Maintaining performance while reducing supply voltage puts pressure on threshold voltage and leakage. Real devices did not continue the ideal scaling relationships indefinitely. Once voltage and other properties no longer scale together, constant power density no longer follows. Power delivery and heat removal then constrain feasible operating points: the **power wall** is an engineering constraint, not a universal frequency or wattage limit.

## Why more cores instead?

For a hypothetical CPU-bound workload, hold per-core activity, capacitance, IPC and work per instruction fixed; ignore shared-system power, communication and leakage. Take one core at frequency f and voltage V, using switching power P. Now build two cores, each at 0.85 f and 0.85 V:

```
one core:   perf 1.00   power 1.00
two cores:  perf 1.70   power 2 x 0.61
                              = 1.23
```

If the work splits across both cores perfectly, you get 1.7× the throughput for 1.23× the power. If a single-core 1.7× clock increase also required 1.7× voltage, this model would predict 1.7³ ≈ 4.9× switching power. That hypothetical scaling is not a claim that such an operating point is feasible or universally impossible to cool.

Multicore can improve aggregate throughput per watt when work can run concurrently, including independent jobs. It does not automatically accelerate one serial task; algorithmic and single-core improvements still matter.

## Amdahl's law

The catch is that most programs are not perfectly parallel. For a fixed-size job, let p be the fraction of its single-core execution time that scales perfectly over n equally fast cores. Assume unchanged serial time and no communication, scheduling, contention or other parallel overhead:

```
speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)
```

```python
def amdahl(p, n):
    if (not 0 <= p <= 1
            or type(n) is not int or n < 1):
        raise ValueError("bad p/n")
    return 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)

for n in (2, 4, 8, 64, 10**9):
    print(n, round(amdahl(0.9, n), 2))
# 2 1.82
# 4 3.08
# 8 4.71
# 64 8.77
# 1000000000 10.0
```

Even with 90% parallel code, 8 cores give only 4.7×, and no number of cores gets past 1 / (1 − p) = 10×. The serial 10% dominates. This shows why serial performance still matters for this workload. Other workloads can justify many smaller cores; the model does not prescribe one chip organisation. (Gustafson's law gives a more hopeful view when the problem size grows with the machine; that is covered in the parallel hardware module.)

## Living within a power budget

Performance per watt is one important CPU design objective, alongside latency, throughput, cost and other constraints. The main techniques:

### Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)

DVFS changes operating frequency and voltage at runtime within supported operating points. Lowering voltage can substantially reduce switching power; frequency changes alone are not governed by a universal cubic law. The best setting depends on workload demands and total energy, including how long execution lasts.

### Turbo boost

Supported processors can raise frequency above a specified base level when power, current, thermal and other limits allow. The available boost depends on the processor and active-core configuration; boost can involve multiple or all active cores, and idle cores need not all be power-gated. Maximum advertised boost is not a guarantee for every workload.

### Race to idle

Sometimes it is better to run fast and then enter a lower-power idle state, because completing work can permit more components to become idle. Whether racing or pacing wins depends on how much static power the rest of the system burns while the work is running.

### Power gating and clock gating

Clock gating suppresses clock transitions and associated switching activity; it does not remove leakage or necessarily prevent every data-driven transition. Power gating disconnects selected supply domains to reduce leakage, with transition costs and possible state-retention requirements. Neither implies that the whole system consumes zero power.

### Heterogeneous cores

Heterogeneous processors combine cores with different performance and energy characteristics. An energy-aware scheduler can use workload demand and an energy model to choose placement, subject to affinity, ISA compatibility, policy and available capacity. A background task is not guaranteed to consume less energy on any core simply labelled “efficient”; evaluate the actual workload and system.

## Dark silicon

**Dark silicon** describes a power-constrained inability to use all available circuitry simultaneously at full performance. The 2011 study by Esmaeilzadeh and colleagues modelled such limits; its projections are not measurements of every current chip or proof that a fixed fraction must be physically powered off at every instant.

Specialised units can perform supported workloads with less instruction-processing overhead or more suitable data paths than general-purpose cores. Benefits depend on utilisation, data movement, programmability and implementation. Idle units may be gated; no universal efficiency multiplier or idle-power figure is established here.

## The bigger picture

Clock frequency, IPC, parallel execution and specialised hardware all contribute to performance. Their importance varies by workload. More cores or an accelerator help only when software and data movement can use them effectively.

> [!warning] Power is a software problem too
> Busy-waiting, polling loops and unnecessary wake-ups keep cores out of their low-power states. On battery-powered devices and in data centres (where electricity and cooling are a large part of running costs), efficient code is measured in watts as well as seconds.

## Key takeaways
- Capacitive switching power is approximately a × C × V² × f; cubic frequency scaling requires an extra voltage-frequency assumption.
- Ideal Dennard scaling keeps power density constant; its breakdown increases the importance of power and thermal budgets.
- Multicore can improve throughput for concurrent work, without automatically speeding up a serial job.
- Fixed-work Amdahl speedup approaches 1 / (1 − p) for p < 1; p = 1 has no finite ceiling in that ideal model.
- DVFS, boost, gating, heterogeneous placement and specialisation have workload-dependent power and energy tradeoffs.

## Further reading
- [Dennard scaling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennard_scaling)
- [The Free Lunch Is Over, by Herb Sutter](http://www.gotw.ca/publications/concurrency-ddj.htm)
- [Dark silicon — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_silicon)
- [Processor power dissipation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Processor_power_dissipation)
- [Amdahl's law — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)
- [ARM big.LITTLE — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARM_big.LITTLE)

- [CMOS Power Consumption (Texas Instruments)](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/scaa035b/scaa035b.pdf)
- [Dark Silicon and the End of Multicore Scaling (original 2011 paper)](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~18742/papers/Esmaeilzadeh2011.pdf)
- [Intel processor technology definitions](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/support/articles/000006513/processors.html)
- [Linux Energy Aware Scheduling](https://kernel.org/doc/html/latest/scheduler/sched-energy.html)
- [Original Dennard et al. scaling paper (1974)](https://stanford.edu/class/cs114/readings/dennard.pdf)

questions.prompt: Using P = a × C × V² × f, what happens to dynamic power if you double the clock frequency but somehow keep the voltage the same?

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: Correct. With a, C and V fixed, power is proportional to f. (In practice a higher f usually needs a higher V too, which makes it much worse.)

options.text: It quadruples
options.explanation: That would be the effect of doubling V, which is squared. Frequency appears only to the first power.

options.text: It rises eightfold
options.explanation: Eightfold follows if both voltage and frequency double while activity and capacitance remain fixed. Only frequency doubles here.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: Each extra cycle switches the transistors again, costing more energy per second.

questions.workedExample: Holding activity, capacitance and voltage fixed, doubling frequency doubles the modelled switching power. A real operating point may require a voltage change, but its size and feasibility require device data.

questions.prompt: Why did power constraints make continuing rapid CPU clock scaling harder around the mid-2000s?

options.text: Transistors stopped getting smaller
options.explanation: Transistors kept shrinking for many more generations; transistor counts kept rising.

options.text: Voltage and device properties no longer followed ideal constant-field scaling, making power density and heat removal stronger constraints
options.explanation: Correct. Reduced voltage scaling and leakage constraints undermined the ideal constant-power-density model. This is not a universal voltage floor, cooling limit or 4 GHz ceiling.

options.text: Software could not use faster clocks
options.explanation: CPU-bound code can benefit from faster clocks, though memory and I/O waits may limit gains. The issue here is feasible power and thermal operation.

options.text: The speed of light limits clocks to 4 GHz
options.explanation: Signal propagation matters for chip design, but it is not what set the plateau; power and heat were.

questions.workedExample: Ideal scaling reduces dimensions and voltage together. Real-device voltage, threshold and leakage constraints prevent indefinite continuation of those relationships. Raising frequency then consumes more of the available power and thermal budget. This encouraged multicore and efficiency work, while clocks and per-core performance continued improving.

questions.prompt: 80% of a program can be spread perfectly across cores; the rest is serial. What is the speedup on 4 cores? Use fixed-work Amdahl assumptions: equal core speeds and no added parallel overhead.

options.explanation: That assumes 100% parallel code. The serial 20% still takes the same time.
This multiplies 0.8 × 4. Amdahl's law divides the time instead.
Correct. Time = 0.2 + 0.8 / 4 = 0.4 of the original, so speedup = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.
5× is the limit with infinitely many cores, 1 / 0.2.

questions.workedExample:
Amdahl: speedup = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / n).

```
serial:   1 - 0.8     = 0.2
parallel: 0.8 / 4     = 0.2
total time            = 0.4
speedup = 1 / 0.4     = 2.5
```

With infinitely many cores, the parallel part shrinks to 0 and the speedup caps at 1 / 0.2 = 5.

questions.prompt: A phone lowers a core's voltage and frequency by 10% each. Roughly how much dynamic power does it save? Assume unchanged activity and capacitance.

options.text: About 27%
options.explanation: Correct: 0.9² × 0.9 = 0.729, so switching power falls 27.1%. This does not establish the change in workload performance or total energy.
That would be true if only f fell. Voltage falls too, and it is squared.
This is the V² effect alone (0.9² = 0.81) and forgets the lower frequency.
Overestimates: 0.9³ is 0.729, not 0.5.

questions.workedExample:
1. P ∝ V² × f.
2. New V = 0.9 V, new f = 0.9 f.
3. P_new / P_old = 0.9² × 0.9 = 0.729.
4. Saving = 1 − 0.729 ≈ **27%**.
5. This is a switching-power estimate; leakage, execution duration and the rest of the system determine total energy.

questions.prompt: Under ideal Dennard scaling, a process shrink scales every dimension and the voltage by k = 0.7. What happens to power per unit area?

options.text: It roughly halves
options.explanation: Power per transistor roughly halves (0.7² = 0.49), but twice as many transistors fit in the same area.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: Correct. Power per transistor scales by k² = 0.49 and transistors per area by 1 / k² ≈ 2.04, so their product is 1.

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: A voltage that fails to scale invalidates the constant-density derivation, but does not imply an exact doubling without assumptions about capacitance, activity and frequency.

options.text: It rises by 1 / k ≈ 1.43
options.explanation: That is the frequency gain, not the change in power density.

questions.workedExample:
Power per transistor = C × V² × f:

```
C: x0.7   V^2: x0.49   f: x1/0.7
C V^2 f = 0.7 x 0.49 / 0.7 = 0.49
```

Transistors per area: 1 / 0.7² ≈ 2.04.

Power per area = 0.49 × 2.04 ≈ **1.0**: constant. This is the ideal constant-field result at unchanged activity, not a guarantee for every real process generation.

questions.prompt: Instead of one core at full voltage and frequency, a designer uses two cores, each at 80% of the voltage and 80% of the frequency. For perfectly parallel work, what are the throughput and dynamic power relative to the single core? Assume per-core activity, capacitance and IPC are unchanged, CPU-bound throughput follows frequency, and exclude leakage and shared-system overhead.

options.text: Throughput 2×, power 2×
options.explanation: The cores run at 80% frequency, so each does 0.8 of the work; and the lower voltage cuts power sharply.

options.text: Throughput 1.6×, power 1.6×
options.explanation: This scales power linearly with frequency and forgets that voltage, which is squared, also fell.

options.text: Throughput 1.28×, power 0.51×
options.explanation: 1.28 would be 1.6 × 0.8, double-counting the slowdown, and 0.51 is the power of one slowed core, not two.

options.text: Throughput 1.6×, power about 1.02×
options.explanation: Correct. Each core does 0.8 of the work rate, so two give 1.6×. Each uses 0.8³ = 0.512 of the power, so two use 1.024×.

questions.workedExample: Each core has relative throughput 0.8 and switching power 0.8² × 0.8 = 0.512. Two cores give throughput 1.6 and power 1.024: 60% more throughput for 2.4% more modelled switching power. A hypothetical single-core 1.6× frequency and voltage increase would cost 1.6³ = 4.096× switching power; feasibility is not established.

questions.prompt: Which statements about power management in modern CPUs are true?

options.text: Supported turbo boost can let busy cores exceed base frequency when operating limits allow
options.explanation: True. Power, current, temperature and product limits govern boost; it can apply to multiple active cores too.

options.text: Clock gating removes leakage power from idle units
options.explanation: False. Clock gating reduces clock-driven switching but does not remove leakage. Power gating can reduce leakage in selected domains.

options.text: DVFS changes voltage and frequency while the system is running
options.explanation: True. DVFS adjusts supported voltage/frequency operating points at runtime; exact policy and update rate vary.

options.text: Heterogeneous designs pair fast cores with small efficient cores so the OS can match tasks to them
options.explanation: True as a heterogeneous-design strategy. Actual scheduling depends on demand, energy models, compatibility, affinity and policy.

options.text: A higher clock always costs proportionally more energy per task
options.explanation: False. Energy per task depends on the voltage needed and on static power. Racing to idle can sometimes use less total energy than running slowly.

questions.workedExample:
Check each against how the mechanisms work:

1. Turbo: shared budget, boosts busy cores. **True.**
2. Clock gating: suppresses clock-driven switching; leakage and some other activity can remain. **False.**
3. DVFS: run-time V/f changes. **True.**
4. Heterogeneous cores: **True.**
5. Energy per task isn't simply proportional to f; static power and race-to-idle complicate it. **False.**

questions.prompt: A data-processing job is 95% parallelisable. You can buy a 16-core or a 64-core server. What speedups does Amdahl's law predict, and what is the ceiling? Assume equal per-core speed, fixed work and no parallel overhead; p is the fraction of original single-core execution time.

options.text: 16× and 64×, no ceiling
options.explanation: This ignores the serial 5%, which takes the same time however many cores there are.

options.text: About 15.2× and 60.8×
options.explanation: This multiplies the core count by 0.95, which is not how Amdahl's law works.

options.text: About 9.1× and 9.1×; more cores never help
options.explanation: More cores do help, just with diminishing returns: 64 cores are about 1.7× better than 16 here.

options.text: About 9.1× and 15.4×, with a ceiling of 20×

questions.workedExample:
```
16 cores: 0.05 + 0.95/16 = 0.1094
          speedup = 9.14
64 cores: 0.05 + 0.95/64 = 0.0648
          speedup = 15.4
limit:    1 / 0.05 = 20
```

1. Quadrupling the cores improves speedup only by 15.4 / 9.14 ≈ 1.7×.
2. If the same workload could instead have parallelisable fraction 97.5%, the ideal ceiling would be 40×. Whether that change is feasible or cost-effective needs separate evidence.

questions.prompt: Product wants a single-threaded workload 20% faster. Option A: raise the clock 20% (voltage must rise proportionally). Option B: a microarchitectural change gives 20% more IPC at the same clock and voltage, for about 10% more dynamic power from extra logic. Roughly how much dynamic power does each need? Hold instruction count fixed and assume CPU-bound performance in both options; keep activity and capacitance fixed for A.

options.text: Both about 1.2×
options.explanation: Option A ignores the voltage increase. Since V is squared, power rises far more than frequency.

options.text: A about 1.44×, B about 1.1×
options.explanation: 1.44 is the V² effect alone; frequency also rose, so it is 1.2³.

options.text: A about 1.73×, B about 1.1×
options.explanation: Correct. A: 1.2 × 1.2² = 1.728. B: same V and f, with roughly 10% more switched capacitance. B gives the same speed for much less power.

options.text: A about 1.1×, B about 1.73×
options.explanation: The values are swapped under the explicit assumptions. Other designs can have different voltage, activity and capacitance tradeoffs.

questions.workedExample:
Option A: P ∝ V² × f.

```
f x1.2, V x1.2
P x 1.2^2 x 1.2 = 1.728
```

Option B: f and V unchanged; extra logic adds about 10% to a × C, so P ≈ 1.1×.

1. Same 20% speedup (iron law: f up 20% vs IPC up 20%).
2. A costs about 73% more power, B about 10%.
3. This model illustrates one incentive to improve IPC and efficiency; clock-rate improvements also continued where operating constraints allowed.

questions.prompt: For a compatible background job without a tight deadline, measurements show lower total energy on an efficiency core. Why might the OS choose it while a performance core is idle?

options.text: Efficiency cores are faster for background work
options.explanation: The given evidence concerns energy, not a guarantee that an efficiency core is faster.

options.text: Performance cores can't run background threads
options.explanation: The compatible task is not inherently prohibited on a performance core; placement also depends on affinity and scheduling policy.

options.text: Efficiency cores use a different instruction set that suits I/O
options.explanation: No I/O-specific instruction set follows from the core label. The question states that the task is compatible.

options.text: It meets the job’s requirements using less measured total energy and may allow the idle performance core to stay in a low-power state
options.explanation: Correct under the supplied measurements. This is a workload-specific tradeoff, not a guarantee based only on the core’s name.

questions.workedExample: The scheduler balances demand, energy and policy. Here the task tolerates its measured completion time and consumes less total energy on the efficiency core. An idle performance core may remain in a low-power state. Exact gating, leakage and migration behaviour depend on the platform.

questions.prompt: Which statements about dark silicon and specialisation are true?

options.text: Dark silicon refers to a power budget that prevents all circuitry from running at full performance simultaneously
options.explanation: True. This does not specify that a fixed fraction is physically powered off at every instant.

options.text: Dark silicon is caused by manufacturing defects that leave parts of the die unusable
options.explanation: False. It is a power and thermal limit on working transistors, not a yield problem.

options.text: Specialised units can improve performance per watt for workloads that suit their implementation
options.explanation: True. Tailored data paths and reduced instruction-processing overhead can help; data movement and utilisation still matter.

options.text: Selective use of specialised accelerators can be one way to use area under a constrained power budget
options.explanation: True as a design option. Area, idle leakage, transition costs and workload benefit must still be evaluated.

options.text: The end of Dennard scaling meant transistor counts stopped increasing
options.explanation: False. Ideal constant-field power scaling and historical transistor-count trends are distinct. Breakdown of the former does not imply that transistor count stops increasing or that power per transistor can never fall again.

questions.workedExample: Dark silicon concerns power-constrained utilisation, not defective circuitry. Specialised accelerators can offer useful tradeoffs for suitable workloads; they are not universally faster or cheaper in energy. The end of ideal Dennard scaling is distinct from the historical trend in transistor counts.
